Control panel & kiosk display for a real dartboard

FlightDeck

One screen for whoever is running the night, a second for the big display everyone actually watches. Eleven games, real scoring off a real board, and a viewer built to be left running on a TV all evening.

v0.23.0 Node 18+ · MIT Scolia · Autodarts · OpenDarts Viewer drawn for 1920×1080

How it is laid out

Two screens, one match

The operator drives everything from Control. The Viewer never needs touching — it just renders whatever the match is currently doing.

Eleven games

Each game owns its own screen

Not a scoreboard with different rules bolted on — every game draws its own viewport, with its own art, pacing and vocabulary. The labels below are the ones the viewer actually prints between rounds.

The bit that makes a room react

Moments, not just scores

Winning, busting and closing a number each get their own screen. Any of them can play a video clip instead of a text overlay — shown here with clips switched off.

Running the night

Set up once, then forget it

Underneath

What it talks to

Boards
Scolia, Autodarts and OpenDarts, picked per venue. A mock board ships too, so a fresh clone plays every game end to end with no hardware at all.
Dart callouts
Every dart can be called on screen, aloud, both or neither. Two voices, generated locally with Kokoro TTS rather than lifted from anywhere.
Config
Everything venue-specific lives in data/ — and none of it is written until you change something, so improved defaults still reach an install that never touched them.
Players
A roster with avatars captured from the browser. HTTPS is not optional here: the camera needs a secure context, so it generates its own certificate on first run.
  • Each game is two files — one for rules and timing, one for its screen — registered in one place.
  • The viewer is drawn for a 1920×1080 kiosk display and expects to run fullscreen.
  • ./run.sh checks for node, npm and openssl, then supervises the server and restarts it if it exits.

Every screenshot on this page is the real application at 1920×1080, driven against the mock board. Player names and avatars are examples, not a real roster, and the camera shows a drawn figure, not a person.

A personal fan project, inspired by Flight Club — not affiliated with or endorsed by them. Some game names (Killer, Shanghai, Cricket, X01) are standard pub-darts terms that predate any single venue.
